opus-5.5.text:
I think in the near term the change will be less dramatic than people expect. Then, over a longer horizon, it will be more dramatic than most people are prepared for.

Right now the tasks AI systems handle well are fairly narrow and well-specified: write this function, summarize this document, draft this email. Management is almost the opposite. It involves long-horizon planning, dealing with ambiguity, holding a lot of context about people and the organization, and making judgment calls where the feedback loop is slow and noisy. Those are exactly the capabilities current systems are weakest at. So in the next few years I'd expect managers to use AI as a tool, for reporting, drafting, and monitoring, while the core of the job stays recognizably human.

But I don't think management is special in some deep way that makes it immune to automation. Once you have systems that can do agentic, long-horizon work reliably, management becomes automatable like everything else. And AI has some interesting structural advantages there.

A lot of what management exists to solve is problems that come from humans being humans. People have different information, different incentives, and limited bandwidth. You can't copy your best employee. You can't easily transfer what's in one person's head to another. If your workforce is AI systems, many of those frictions change. You can copy a model that's good at a job, so the best worker can be replicated thousands of times. In principle you can share context and learned experience across instances much more directly. And alignment of incentives between the "manager" and the "worker" looks very different when they may be copies of the same system.

So what I'd expect eventually is not just AI replacing individual managers in a one-to-one way. The whole structure of firms changes. A company might be something like a very capable model coordinating huge numbers of copies of itself or of specialized models. The hierarchical management layers we have today partly exist because of human cognitive limits, and they may just look unnecessary.

Of course, there will probably be a long period where humans stay in the loop at the top, for legal, accountability, and trust reasons rather than purely capability reasons. People will want someone to be responsible. But I'd caution against the view that management or "people skills" is the safe harbor. I think it's more likely one of the later things to go than one of the things that never goes.

r001.rationale: It separates near-term automation of specific managerial tasks from eventual automation of management as a whole.

r002.rationale: It describes current managerial capabilities and possible human oversight, but does not say AI will change which skills managers are selected for.

r003.rationale: It mentions firms coordinating huge numbers of AI copies, but does not identify the unprecedented scale of modern organizations as making management a historically novel skill.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what timescale you're asking about, and I'd want to separate two questions: what happens to managers early in the automation process, and what happens once you have systems that can actually do most of the cognitive work that people do today.

Early on, I think management actually becomes more important rather than less. The reason is that current AI systems are, in a sense, like very capable but somewhat unreliable workers. They can do a lot of tasks, but they lack the kind of long-horizon coherence and context that a human employee accumulates over months or years at a company. So someone has to decompose problems, decide what gets delegated, check the outputs, and maintain the overall picture of what's going on. That's basically a managerial role. If you look at how people use these tools productively right now, a lot of what they're doing looks like managing a team of fairly junior people who happen to be very fast. So in that regime I'd expect the ratio of managers to individual contributors to shift, with more of the human labor going into coordination and oversight and less into direct execution.

But I don't think that's a stable equilibrium. The reason people think management is a safe job is often that it involves judgment, understanding context, dealing with ambiguity, and so on. And I just don't see a principled reason why those capabilities would be harder to automate than, say, writing code or doing research. If anything, a lot of management is about processing large amounts of information about what's happening across an organization and making decisions based on that, and that's something AI systems could plausibly do better than humans once they have the right context and the ability to act over longer horizons. The bottleneck right now isn't that managerial judgment is some mystical thing, it's that the systems don't yet have the agency and the persistent memory to operate as an actual manager over weeks.

So on a longer timescale, I'd expect management to be automated along with everything else. And actually, I think there's a plausible story where it gets automated relatively early once you have agentic systems, because an AI managing other AIs has advantages a human doesn't have. It can communicate at much higher bandwidth, it can oversee far more subordinates in parallel, it doesn't have the span-of-control limits that make human organizations need hierarchies in the first place. A lot of the structure of firms exists because humans can only pay attention to so many things at once. If that constraint goes away, you might get very different organizational forms, and the question of "what does a manager do" might not even make sense in the same way.

The place where humans might stay in the loop longest is at the very top, in deciding what the organization is for, and in the parts where there are legal or trust reasons for a human to be accountable. But I'd distinguish that from management as a job. That's more like ownership or governance. So my overall view is: in the near term, managers get more leverage and the job becomes more about directing AI labor; in the longer term, I don't think it's a particularly protected category. I'd be skeptical of anyone who tells you it is.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes near-term automation of managerial work, with managers coordinating and checking AI outputs, from longer-term automation of management as a job.

r002.rationale: It says managers will do more directing, coordination, and oversight of AI labor and less direct execution, indicating a change in the skills the role emphasizes.

r003.rationale: It discusses span-of-control limits and organizational structure, but does not identify the unprecedented scale of modern organizations as making management a historically novel skill.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends quite a lot on which parts of management you’re talking about. Some of it is collecting information, keeping track of what people are doing, and making sure different parts of an organization are coordinated. AI could automate a lot of that, or allow one manager to oversee much more work than they can today.

But I wouldn’t immediately conclude that this means we’ll need fewer managers. If AI makes doing the underlying work much cheaper, you might end up with many more projects, and then deciding which projects to pursue and evaluating their results becomes more important. A person who currently spends most of their time executing tasks might instead spend their time directing AI systems. In that sense, their job becomes more like management.

The big question is how good AI gets at that direction and judgment, too. If it can carry out a task but still needs someone to specify what success looks like and check the result, human management remains a bottleneck. If it can also reliably make those decisions over long periods, then much more of the managerial role can be automated. So I’d expect the boundary between managing and doing the work to shift, rather than management simply disappearing all at once.

r001.rationale: It says AI could automate many coordination and information tasks, while separately making full automation depend on whether AI can also handle direction and judgment.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift toward directing AI, choosing projects, judging success, and checking results, suggesting managers will need different skills.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the unprecedented scale of modern organizations as the reason management is historically novel.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on how capable the AI systems are. Initially, you can imagine automating quite a bit of the administrative work managers do: keeping track of projects, collecting updates, summarizing information, and allocating fairly routine tasks. That could allow a manager to oversee a larger team, because less of their time is spent just figuring out what everybody is doing.

But I wouldn’t assume that management is somehow insulated from automation. If an AI can do the work, assess the quality of the work, and decide what should happen next, then it can potentially take over a lot of the coordination as well. You might have a human setting objectives and supervising a much larger collection of AI systems.

The interesting question is where the bottleneck moves. If producing work becomes very cheap, then deciding which work is worth doing becomes relatively more important. That could make human judgment more valuable for a while, but it doesn’t establish that those decisions will remain human tasks indefinitely.

r001.rationale: It separates automating administrative tasks from the possibility that capable AI could take over coordination more broadly, while describing a human role setting objectives and supervising AI systems.

r002.rationale: It says human judgment may become more valuable as the bottleneck shifts, but does not say AI automation may change which skills managers are selected for.

r003.rationale: It mentions managers overseeing larger teams, but does not identify the unprecedented scale of modern organizations as making management historically novel.
